subject.title: The Glove and the Lions
subject.author: Leigh Hunt

title: The King's Verdict Nobody Else Ever Recorded
standfirst: The anecdote behind this poem survives as one flat sentence, set down by a court memoirist who was a small child when it supposedly happened. Leigh Hunt gave it a moral nobody had ever attached to it before — and two other poets, one before him and one after, gave it two more.

sections.heading: A Memoirist Who Wasn't in the Room
sections.body:
Long before Francis I got a speaking part in anyone's poem, this story existed as a single sentence in someone else's memoirs, and it carried no moral at all. The earliest known account comes from [Brantôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Bourdeille,_seigneur_de_Brant%C3%B4me), a court chronicler born around 1540 — which made him at most a small child when Francis I died in 1547, too young to have witnessed a lion pit at court himself. He wrote his memoirs late in life, after a riding accident forced his retirement around 1589, and they went unpublished until 1665, half a century after his own death.

What survives of his account, [reprinted in English translation](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Poetical_Works_of_Leigh_Hunt/The_Glove_and_the_Lions) as a footnote to Hunt's own poem, runs like this: a lady told the Count de Lorge that if he loved her as much as he swore, he should fetch her dropped glove from among the king's lions. He did, then "threw it in the lady's face," and the account adds only that he "would never see her afterwards." No king interrupts. Nobody hands down a verdict on love against vanity. The story just stops, the way a piece of court gossip stops, and leaves the judging to whoever repeats it next.

sections.heading: Hunt Gives Francis a Speech Nobody Recorded
sections.body:
By the time Leigh Hunt versified Brantôme's one sentence for [the New Monthly Magazine in May 1836](https://rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/glove-and-lions), the anecdote had been circulating in French and English for decades. What Hunt added was an entire extra character's judgement. His King Francis watches the Count throw the glove back "right in the lady's face," then delivers the line every reader of this poem remembers:

> "By God!" said Francis, "rightly done!" and he rose from where he sat:
> "No love," quoth he, "but vanity, sets love a task like that."

That verdict belongs entirely to Hunt. Brantôme's account never mentions the king reacting at all, let alone naming the offence. Hunt built a courtroom onto a piece of gossip that had never asked for one.

He was fifty-one that year, a long way from the circle Keats and Shelley had once gathered him into. He had already served two years in prison, from 1813 to 1815, for [libelling the Prince Regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Hunt) in the *Examiner*, and had strained old loyalties further in 1828 by publishing a memoir of Byron unflattering enough that it read, to many, like biting the hand that had fed him. Through the early 1830s he edited the *Tatler*, a daily paper of literary and dramatic criticism, and watched it fail like the ventures before it. A four-stanza ballad, written for a magazine fee decades after the poetry that made his name, would end up one of the pieces by which he is still best remembered.

sections.heading: Schiller Had Already Rewritten It, With a Bigger Menagerie
sections.body:
Hunt was not even the first poet to add an ending. Nearly forty years earlier, in 1797, Friedrich Schiller turned the same anecdote into ["Der Handschuh"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Handschuh), written during his "Balladenjahr" — a year of friendly rivalry with Goethe in which both poets turned out ballad after ballad. Schiller had found the story in the same French history Hunt would later draw on, and expanded Hunt's plain lions into a whole staged combat: a lion, a tiger, and two leopards, each sized up and left unimpressed by the others before the lady, Fräulein Kunigund, drops her glove among them.

Schiller's knight, Delorges, delivers no line for a king to approve. He retrieves the glove, throws it back at her, and simply leaves — the German reads "Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht!", rendered in the standard English verse translation as "'Nay, spare me the guerdon, at least,' quoth he; / 'And he left for ever that fair ladye!'" There is no court verdict, no public rebuke from a monarch. It is one man's private and permanent withdrawal, not a case Francis gets to close for everyone watching.

sections.heading: Browning Puts the Lady on the Stand
sections.body:
Nine years after Hunt's version appeared, Robert Browning reopened the case. His "The Glove," published in 1845 as the closing poem of *Dramatic Romances and Lyrics* — [the seventh volume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_Romances_and_Lyrics) of his self-published *Bells and Pomegranates* — is narrated by a witness Browning invents for the occasion: the subtitle reads "Peter Ronsard loquitur," putting the words in the mouth of the real sixteenth-century French poet. One scholarly reading of the poem, examining Browning's sources, has noted flatly that this is roughly where [Hunt's own poem ends](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/victorian-literature-and-culture/article/abs/glove-and-the-poets/3545497C91AD556DBB3BA402D809DA4A) — Browning picks the story up at the thrown glove and keeps going.

What follows is the defence nobody had given the lady before. Ronsard finds her afterward, and she explains herself directly: ["Too long had I heard / Of the deed proved alone by the word"](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Glove) — she wanted proof harder than a courtier's promise, and got it. Browning does not let Hunt's tidy ending stand, either: the lady marries, "and to that marriage some happiness, maugre / The voice of the Court, I dared augur," while De Lorge goes on to court and win a new favourite of the king's — though the King, tellingly, never again asks him to fetch anyone's dropped glove.

sections.heading: The Word Hunt Can't Stop Repeating
sections.body:
Set next to Schiller's private walk-off and Browning's cross-examination, Hunt's own choice looks sharper: he wants a public verdict, and he builds his stanzas to sound like one arriving. Each of his four sextets runs in tight rhymed couplets, long rolling lines closer to an old fourteener than to anything dainty, so that the whole poem has the bounce of a ballad being sung rather than solemnly read.

Into that bounce he packs a single word until it stops meaning anything steady. The last stanza alone runs: she drops her glove "to prove his love," he leaps in and returns, and throws the glove back "but not with love"; the king then closes with "no love ... but vanity, sets love a task like that." Four uses of one word in six lines, each one narrowing what counts as love a little further, until Francis gets to define it for everyone by simply being the last to say it. The rhythm does the same work as the verdict: it forecloses.
